lessons.title: Identifying Your Target Customers: Tourists, Locals, or Bars
lessons.body:
Before you brew a single batch, decide who will drink it. In Africa, your customers fall into three main groups: tourists, locals, and bars/restaurants. Tourists (both domestic and international) often look for authentic, unique experiences. They will pay a premium for a storyâlike a gin made with local botanicals or a wine from a specific region. Locals are your steady base. They buy regularly, often in larger quantities, and care about price, consistency, and taste. Bars, restaurants, and hotels buy in bulk but expect reliability, invoicing, and sometimes exclusivity.

Start by mapping your area. If you are near a national park or a popular beach, tourists are a key segment. If you are in a residential neighborhood, locals will be your bread and butter. If you are in a city center, bars and restaurants are within reach. Visit 10 potential customers and ask: What do you sell? What do your customers ask for? What is missing? For example, a lodge in Kenya might want a honey wine (mead) for international guests, while a local bar in Ghana might want a affordable, strong gin.

Use simple data. Count foot traffic past your location at different times. Check social media groups for expats or tourists in your region. Look at what competitors sell and at what price. A common mistake is trying to serve everyone. Instead, pick one primary segment for your first year. If you choose tourists, you might package in 375ml bottles with a story on the label and sell at $10â$15. If locals, you might sell 750ml bottles at $3â$5. If bars, you might offer kegs or cases at wholesale prices.

Once you choose, tailor everything: your bottle size, your price, your label, your sales pitch. For tourists, highlight local ingredients and traditional methods. For locals, emphasize value and taste. For bars, focus on profit margins and reliability. You can expand later, but mastering one segment first builds cash flow and reputation.

lessons.title: Selling to Bars, Restaurants, and Hotels: Pitching and Sampling
lessons.body:
Getting your drinks into bars, restaurants, and hotels can transform your business. These venues buy in volume and pay consistently, but they need to trust you. Start by researching which venues already sell craft or local drinks. Walk in during off-peak hours (mid-afternoon) and ask to speak to the manager or owner. Bring a sample bottle, a price list, and a one-page info sheet about your product.

Your pitch should be short and focused on their profit. For example: "This is a 750ml bottle of my hibiscus gin. I sell it to you for $8. You can sell it by the shot for $4, making $32 per bottle. It's unique, locally made, and your customers will love the story." Always lead with the margin. Bars care about how much they can make. If you can, offer a free sample bottle for them to try with staff. Staff recommendations drive sales.

Sampling is your best tool. Organize a tasting for the bar staff after hours. Bring small cups and let them taste your gin, wine, or cider neat and in a simple cocktail. Explain the flavor notes and how it's made. Leave behind a few bottles at cost for them to feature as a special. If they sell out, they will reorder. Follow up within one week. Ask: "How did the staff like it? Did customers ask for it?" If yes, ask for a regular order.

Hotels and restaurants often require invoices, delivery schedules, and sometimes exclusivity. Be prepared to provide these. A simple invoice book from a local stationery shop works. Offer delivery twice a week. If they want exclusivity, negotiate a minimum order. For example, you won't sell to their competitor within 2km if they order 10 cases per month. Always deliver on time and in good condition. One late delivery can lose a client. Build relationships: remember names, bring small gifts on holidays, and be reliable.

lessons.title: Using Social Media: WhatsApp, Instagram, and Facebook for Brewers
lessons.body:
Social media is the cheapest and most effective way to sell your drinks in Africa. WhatsApp is king for direct sales. Create a WhatsApp Business account (free) and set up a catalog with photos, prices, and descriptions. Share your status daily with photos of your brewing process, new batches, and happy customers. Use broadcast lists to send updates to customers who opt in. For example, "New batch of ginger beer ready! 750ml for $4. Order now for delivery tomorrow." Respond quicklyâwithin an hour if possible. Use WhatsApp groups for loyal customers and offer them a 10% discount for referrals.

Instagram is for visual storytelling. Post high-quality photos of your bottles, your brewery, and your events. Use hashtags like #AfricanCraftBeer, #GinAfrica, #LocalWine. Tag your location. Post 3â4 times a week. Use Stories to show behind-the-scenes: bottling, labeling, or a tasting event. Go Live during a tasting to engage followers. You can also run simple ads for as little as $5 to target people in your city who like craft beer or wine. Instagram is great for attracting tourists and expats.

Facebook is for community and events. Create a business page and join local groups (e.g., "Nairobi Foodies" or "Cape Town Craft Beer Enthusiasts"). Share your posts there, but don't spamâengage genuinely. Use Facebook Events to promote tastings at markets or festivals. You can also use Facebook Marketplace to sell directly, though check local regulations. For all platforms, consistency matters. Post at least 3 times a week. Use a simple phone camera and natural light. Show your faceâpeople buy from people. Ask customers to tag you in their posts and offer a small reward (e.g., a free bottle) for user-generated content. Track what works: use WhatsApp to ask customers how they heard about you, and note which posts get the most orders.

lessons.title: Hosting Tastings at Markets and Festivals
lessons.body:
Tastings are the fastest way to get new customers. Markets and festivals attract people already in a buying mood. Start by finding local events: farmers markets, food festivals, music festivals, or cultural days. Contact the organizer earlyâat least one month aheadâand ask about vendor fees. In many African cities, a stall at a weekend market costs $20â$50 per day. Festivals may charge $100â$300. Book a spot with good foot traffic, preferably near food stalls.

Your stall should be simple but inviting. Bring a folding table, a bright tablecloth, and a banner with your brand name and logo. Use a cooler with ice to keep drinks cold. Offer small tasting cups (30ml) for free or a token price (e.g., $0.50). Have bottles for sale at a special event price. For example, sell 750ml bottles at $5 instead of $7. Display a sign with prices and a QR code to your WhatsApp or Instagram. Bring a friend to helpâone person pours, the other talks and handles money.

When tasting, engage the customer. Ask: "Do you prefer dry or sweet?" or "Have you tried a local gin before?" Explain what makes your drink specialâthe ingredients, the process, the story. Don't just pour and stay silent. Collect contact details: have a notebook or a simple Google Form on a tablet. Offer a free bottle for every 10 people who sign up for your WhatsApp list. At the end of the day, count your sales and note what worked. Did people prefer the wine or the gin? Did they ask for a specific size? Use this feedback to plan your next batch.

Follow up within 48 hours. Send a WhatsApp message to everyone who signed up: "Thanks for tasting at [event]! Here's a 10% discount on your first order." This turns a one-time taster into a repeat customer. Tastings also build your reputationâpeople talk about the friendly brewer they met. Over time, you can become a regular at the best events.

lessons.title: Building a Route to Market: Distributors vs. Direct Delivery
lessons.body:
Once you have steady production, you need a reliable way to get your drinks to customers. You have two main options: distributors or direct delivery. Distributors are companies that buy your product in bulk and sell it to bars, shops, and restaurants. They take a cut (typically 20â30% of retail price) but handle logistics, storage, and sales. This is good if you produce large volumes and don't want to spend time driving around. However, you lose control over pricing and customer relationships. To find distributors, ask other local brewers, attend trade shows, or search online for "beverage distributor [your city]".

Direct delivery means you sell and deliver yourself. This gives you higher margins and direct feedback. You can start with a simple route: visit 10 bars or shops per day, take orders, and deliver the next day. Use a motorbike, car, or even a bicycle with a cooler box. Charge a delivery fee for small orders (e.g., $2) or offer free delivery for orders over $50. Keep a log of customers, order frequency, and payment status. A simple notebook or a free app like Google Sheets works. Direct delivery is best when you are small and want to build relationships.

A hybrid approach often works best. Use direct delivery for your top 20 customers (bars, hotels, loyal individuals) and a distributor for smaller shops and distant areas. For example, you might deliver directly within your city and use a distributor for neighboring towns. Always calculate your costs: fuel, time, packaging. If direct delivery costs you $10 per drop and the order is only $30, you lose money. Set a minimum order for free delivery. Also, consider partnering with other local producers (e.g., a cheese maker or baker) to share delivery routes. This reduces costs and increases drop sizes. Review your route every three months: which customers are profitable? Which take too much time? Adjust accordingly.

lessons.title: Exporting to Neighboring Countries: Documentation and Logistics
lessons.body:
Exporting your drinks to neighboring countries can open new markets, but it requires paperwork and planning. Start by researching the import rules of your target country. For example, Kenya to Uganda, or South Africa to Namibia. You will need: a business license, a tax clearance certificate, a certificate of origin (from your local chamber of commerce), and a health certificate for your product. For alcohol, you often need an import permit from the destination country's revenue authority. Contact their embassy or trade office for a list. In many cases, you also need to register your product with the local standards bureau (e.g., KEBS in Kenya, SABS in South Africa). This can take 2â6 months and cost $200â$500.

Logistics: For small volumes (under 1000 bottles), you can use a courier service like DHL or a regional bus company that carries parcels. For larger volumes, hire a truck or use a freight forwarder. Always pack bottles in sturdy boxes with dividers. Use a customs agent to clear your goods at the borderâthey know the paperwork and can prevent delays. Expect to pay import duties and VAT in the destination country. These can add 30â50% to your cost, so price accordingly.

Start small. Test one neighboring country with a single pallet (e.g., 500 bottles). Work with a local distributor there who can handle customs and sales. Attend a trade fair in that country to find partners. For example, the Zambia Agricultural and Commercial Show or the Nigeria Food and Beverage Fair. Before you export, ensure your product meets labeling laws: include ingredients, alcohol content, volume, and your contact details in the local language if required. Also, check for any bans on certain ingredients. Once you have a successful trial, scale up gradually. Keep records of all shipments, payments, and customs documents for at least five years. Exporting is complex but rewardingâit can double your production and brand recognition.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Taking Your Brew to Market in Africa

This reference module consolidates the practical knowledge needed to move your drinks from the brewhouse to paying customers across African markets. Whether you produce wine, gin, cider, or beer, the commercial challenge is the same: identify who buys, how they buy, and what it costs to reach them profitably. The lessons below cover customer segmentation, trade sales, social media, events, route-to-market, and export logistics â all grounded in African market realities.

1. Identifying Your Target Customers: Tourists, Locals, or Bars

African beverage markets are not monolithic. A craft brewery in Cape Town, a gin distillery in Nairobi, and a palm wine or sorghum beer producer in Accra face very different customer profiles. Three broad segments dominate:

  • Tourists: High willingness to pay for authentic, story-rich products. They buy at hotels, airports, lodges, and tasting rooms. Seasonality is extreme â coastal and safari destinations peak in specific months.
  • Locals: Volume drivers. Price-sensitive but loyal if quality is consistent. They buy through bars, supermarkets, informal retail (kiosks, shebeens, bottle stores), and direct.
  • Bars, restaurants, and hotels (trade): Recurring revenue but require credit terms, reliable delivery, and staff training. One hotel account can equal hundreds of retail customers.

Use the table below to map your product against these segments before you spend money on marketing.

Table 1: Customer Segment Comparison for African Craft Beverage Producers
Factor Tourists Locals Trade (Bars/Hotels)
Price sensitivity Low High Medium (negotiated)
Purchase frequency Seasonal Weekly/daily Weekly/monthly orders
Volume potential Low-medium High High
Payment terms Cash/card Cash/mobile money Credit 30â60 days
Key channel Hotels, airports, lodges Bars, kiosks, supermarkets Direct sales force
Marketing tool Instagram, TripAdvisor WhatsApp, radio, word-of-mouth Sampling, tastings, relationships

Source: Adapted from Euromonitor International, "Alcoholic Drinks in Africa," 2023, and UNWTO Tourism Data Dashboard, 2024.

2. Selling to Bars, Restaurants, and Hotels: Pitching and Sampling

Trade sales are relationship-driven. A bar manager in Lagos or a lodge owner in Livingstone buys from people they trust and who make their life easy. Your pitch must answer three questions: What is it? Why will customers buy it? How do I make money on it?

Bring samples â always. In most African markets, a tasting is worth more than a brochure. Offer a margin structure that works for the venue (typically 25â40% markup), and provide staff training so waiters can recommend your product confidently. Start with independent bars and guesthouses before approaching large hotel groups, which have procurement committees and longer sales cycles.

3. Using Social Media: WhatsApp, Instagram, and Facebook for Brewers

Social media in Africa is mobile-first and increasingly commerce-enabled. Each platform has a distinct role:

  • WhatsApp: The default business communication tool. Use WhatsApp Business for catalogues, order taking, and customer updates. Broadcast lists and status updates replace email newsletters for many SMEs.
  • Instagram: Visual storytelling. Show the brewing process, the people, the place. Reels and Stories drive discovery among urban 18â35s and tourists researching destinations.
  • Facebook: Community and events. Facebook Groups and Events are still dominant for local promotions, market days, and festival announcements in many African countries.

Post consistently, use local languages where appropriate, and always include a clear call to action (WhatsApp link, location, or order number).

4. Hosting Tastings at Markets and Festivals

Markets and festivals are the cheapest customer acquisition channel available to African brewers. A well-run stall at a food market in Kigali or a music festival in Dakar can generate more sales and brand awareness in one weekend than a month of social media posts. Key practices:

  • Secure all permits and licences well in advance â alcohol sampling rules vary by country and municipality.
  • Design a simple, repeatable tasting script for your team.
  • Capture WhatsApp numbers or Instagram handles in exchange for a small discount.
  • Bring enough stock â running out is a lost opportunity and a bad look.

5. Building a Route to Market: Distributors vs. Direct Delivery

Your route-to-market determines your margin, your control, and your growth ceiling. Direct delivery gives you higher margins and customer intimacy but caps your reach at your logistics capacity. Distributors give you reach and bulk orders but take 20â35% margin and often control the customer relationship. Most successful African craft producers start direct, then add distributors for secondary cities or export markets.

Table 2: Route-to-Market Comparison â Direct vs. Distributor vs. Hybrid
Criteria Direct Delivery Distributor Hybrid
Gross margin retained High (80â100%) Low (65â80%) Medium (70â90%)
Geographic reach Limited Wide Wide
Logistics burden High Low Medium
Customer relationship Direct Indirect Mixed
Best for Startups, key accounts Scale, secondary cities Growth-stage producers

Source: Adapted from International Trade Centre (ITC), "Route to Market for SMEs," 2022, and TechnoServe "Africa Agribusiness Toolkit," 2023.

6. Exporting to Neighboring Countries: Documentation and Logistics

Exporting within Africa â for example, from Kenya to Uganda, or from South Africa to Namibia â is often more complex than exporting to Europe because of overlapping regional trade rules. Key requirements:

  • Product registration: Most countries require registration with the national standards body or food safety authority.
  • Export documents: Commercial invoice, packing list, certificate of origin, phytosanitary or health certificate, and customs declaration.
  • Regional trade agreements: Check whether your product qualifies for preferential tariffs under COMESA, SADC, ECOWAS, or the AfCFTA.
  • Logistics: Cold chain, customs clearance agents, and reliable freight forwarders are critical. Budget for delays.

â ï¸ SAFETY WARNING: Alcohol and Regulatory Compliance

Alcohol production and sale is heavily regulated across Africa. Before selling, verify: (1) your production licence and excise duty registration, (2) local municipal trading and sampling permits, (3) health and safety standards for your facility, and (4) age-verification requirements for sales. Selling without proper licences can result in fines, confiscation, or imprisonment. Never sell to minors. Always label products with alcohol content and health warnings as required by your national standards body.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Define your primary customer segment (tourists, locals, or trade) before spending on marketing.
  2. Set a margin structure that works for both you and your trade customers (25â40% markup for venues).
  3. Use WhatsApp Business for orders and customer communication; Instagram for storytelling; Facebook for events.
  4. Run at least one tasting event per quarter at a market or festival to acquire customers directly.
  5. Start with direct delivery for key accounts; add distributors only when logistics capacity is exceeded.
  6. Register your product with the national standards body before exporting to any neighboring country.
  7. Confirm all licences, permits, and excise registrations are current before every sales period.
  8. Track your cost per acquisition and cost per delivery â if either exceeds gross margin, change your route to market.

Further Reading

  • International Trade Centre (ITC) â SME Trade Tools and Market Analysis
  • FAO â Agricultural and Food Business Resources
  • AfCFTA Secretariat â African Continental Free Trade Area Official Resources
  • COMESA â Regional Trade and Export Documentation
  • SADC â Trade and Industrialisation Resources

This module is part of the Rise AFRICA Skills course: Brewery â Wine, Gin, Cider & Beer. All figures and sources are cited for reference and should be verified against current national regulations before commercial use.

quiz.q: Which customer segment is most likely to pay a premium for a unique story about local ingredients?
quiz.explanation: Tourists often seek authentic experiences and are willing to pay more for products with a local story.

quiz.q: When choosing a target customer, what is a recommended first step?
options: A) Brew a large batch of all types
B) Visit 10 potential customers and ask questions
quiz.explanation: Talking directly to potential customers gives you real data on what they want.

quiz.q: What is a common mistake when identifying target customers?
quiz.explanation: Trying to serve everyone dilutes your marketing and can lead to poor results; better to master one segment first.

quiz.q: If you target locals, what bottle size and price might be appropriate?
quiz.explanation: Locals typically look for value and larger sizes at affordable prices.

quiz.q: What should you emphasize when pitching to bars and restaurants?
options: B) The profit margin they can make
D) The color of your label
quiz.explanation: Bars care most about how much money they can make from selling your product.

quiz.q: When is the best time to walk into a bar to pitch your drinks?
quiz.explanation: Off-peak hours allow managers to give you attention without disrupting service.

quiz.q: What is a key element of a successful pitch to a bar?
options: A) A long history of your brewery
B) A free sample and a clear price list
quiz.explanation: Samples let them taste the product, and a price list shows professionalism.

quiz.q: After leaving samples at a bar, how soon should you follow up?
options: D) Never, wait for them to call
quiz.explanation: Following up within a week keeps your product fresh in their mind and shows initiative.

quiz.q: What is a common requirement when selling to hotels?
options: A) Free samples for all guests
B) Invoices and regular delivery schedules
quiz.explanation: Hotels need proper invoicing and reliable delivery to manage their supplies.

quiz.q: Which social media platform is best for direct sales and order-taking in Africa?
quiz.explanation: WhatsApp Business is widely used for direct communication, catalogs, and order processing.

quiz.q: What feature of WhatsApp Business helps you showcase your products?
quiz.explanation: The catalog allows you to list products with photos, prices, and descriptions.

quiz.q: On Instagram, what is a good way to engage followers during a tasting event?
options: A) Post a photo after the event
quiz.explanation: Going Live lets followers see the event in real-time and interact.

quiz.q: What should you do to encourage user-generated content on social media?
options: B) Offer a small reward for tagging you
quiz.explanation: Rewarding customers for tagging you increases reach and social proof.

quiz.q: Which platform is best for promoting local events like tastings?
quiz.explanation: Facebook Events is designed for creating and sharing event details with the local community.

quiz.q: How often should you post on social media to stay visible?
options: B) At least 3 times a week
D) Only when you have a new product
quiz.explanation: Consistent posting at least 3 times a week keeps your audience engaged.

quiz.q: What is a typical cost for a stall at a weekend market in many African cities?
quiz.explanation: Weekend market stalls are relatively affordable, often $20â$50 per day.

quiz.q: At a tasting, what is a good way to collect customer contacts?
options: A) Ask them to write on a napkin
B) Use a notebook or Google Form
C) Take a photo of their ID
quiz.explanation: A simple notebook or digital form makes it easy to follow up later.

quiz.q: What should you do within 48 hours after a tasting event?
options: A) Send a thank-you message with a discount
B) Wait for them to contact you
C) Post photos on social media
D) Start planning the next event
quiz.explanation: Following up quickly with a thank-you and incentive turns tasters into customers.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of using a distributor?
options: C) They handle logistics and sales
quiz.explanation: Distributors take on the work of storage, delivery, and selling to retailers.

quiz.q: What is a typical cut that distributors take?
quiz.explanation: Distributors usually take 20â30% of the retail price for their services.

quiz.q: What is a disadvantage of direct delivery?
quiz.explanation: Direct delivery requires you to spend time and money on transport and logistics.

quiz.q: What is a good minimum order for free delivery?
quiz.explanation: A $50 minimum ensures the delivery cost is covered by the order value.

quiz.q: What is a hybrid route to market?
options: C) Using both direct and distributors
quiz.explanation: A hybrid approach combines direct delivery for key customers and distributors for wider reach.

quiz.q: Why might you partner with other local producers for delivery?
options: A) To share costs and increase drop sizes
quiz.explanation: Sharing delivery routes with complementary producers reduces costs and improves efficiency.

quiz.q: What document is often required for exporting alcohol to a neighboring country?
options: B) An import permit from the destination country
quiz.explanation: Most countries require an import permit for alcoholic beverages.

quiz.q: How long can it take to register your product with a standards bureau?
quiz.explanation: Product registration with bodies like KEBS or SABS typically takes 2â6 months.

quiz.q: What is a cost-effective way to ship small volumes (under 1000 bottles) for export?
quiz.explanation: Courier services like DHL are practical for small export volumes.

quiz.q: What should you expect to pay at the border when exporting?
quiz.explanation: Import duties and VAT are standard and can add 30â50% to your cost.

quiz.q: What is a good first step before exporting to a new country?
options: B) Test with a small shipment
quiz.explanation: Starting with a small trial shipment reduces risk and tests the market.

quiz.q: What labeling information is typically required for exported drinks?
options: B) Ingredients, alcohol content, volume, and contact details
C) A picture of the brewer
D) The price in local currency
quiz.explanation: Most countries require detailed labeling including ingredients, alcohol content, volume, and contact information.
